prompt: When is it decided which overload of `show` a call reaches?
hint: Nothing about overloading happens at run time.

choices.text: At compile time, from the argument types
choices.why: Right: `javac` picks one and writes its choice into the class file.

choices.text: At run time, from the class of the object passed in
choices.why: That describes overriding, chosen by the object while the program runs.

choices.text: When the JIT compiles the method, from how often each one runs
choices.why: The JIT never changes which method a call means; it only speeds up the one chosen.

choices.text: When the class is loaded, from the order the overloads are written
choices.why: The order in the file plays no part.

prompt: `show(small)`, with `byte small = 5`, printed `int 5`. Why not `Integer` or `Object`?
hint: There is no `show(byte)`.

choices.text: Because a `byte` literal is always an `int` in Java
choices.why: `small` is a `byte` variable; the conversion happened at the call.

choices.text: Widening to `int` is preferred over boxing or reaching `Object`
choices.why: Right: the nearest wider primitive wins before any boxing is tried.

choices.text: Because `show(int)` is written first in the class
choices.why: Order in the file never decides.

prompt: When no overload matches exactly, put the compiler's preferences in order, the most preferred first.
hint: `Ranking` asked twice.
items: Widening a primitive, such as `int` to `long`

prompt: Why does widening rank above boxing?
hint: Boxing arrived in Java 5.

choices.text: Because boxing allocates an object and is slower
choices.why: Speed was not the reason the section gave.

choices.text: Because primitives are checked before objects in every Java rule
choices.why: There is no such general rule; this one is about history.

choices.text: So that calls written before Java 5 kept reaching the same method
choices.why: Right: a 1.4 program's `widen(5)` had always reached `widen(long)`, and still does.

prompt: `lend(Integer, Object)` and `lend(Object, Integer)` both exist. What does `lend(1, 2)` do?
hint: Neither path is better than the other.

choices.text: Calls the first method declared
choices.why: The compiler does not pick by position.

choices.text: Calls both, in order
choices.why: One call reaches one method, or none.

choices.text: It does not compile: ambiguous
choices.why: Right: it names both candidates and leaves the choice to you.

choices.text: Throws at run time when the JVM cannot decide
choices.why: It never gets that far; the error is at compile time.

prompt: A method's name and its parameter types, in order, are called its ___; the return type is not part of it.
hint: `Twice` failed because two methods had the same one.

prompt: What is an override?
hint: One level down, same signature.

choices.text: A second method in the same class with the same name and other parameters
choices.why: That is an overload.

choices.text: A subclass's method with the signature of one it inherited
choices.why: Right: it replaces the inherited body for objects of the subclass.

choices.text: Any method marked `@Override`
choices.why: The annotation only asks for a check; the method is an override whether or not it is there.

prompt: `Typo` declared `descibe()` without `@Override`. What did `typo.describe()` print, and why?
hint: A new method nobody calls.

choices.text: `typo Dom Casmurro`, because the compiler corrected the spelling
choices.why: The compiler corrects nothing; it accepted a new method.

choices.text: `item Dom Casmurro`, from `Item`
choices.why: Right: `descibe` replaced nothing, so `Item`'s method ran.

choices.text: Nothing, because the program did not compile
choices.why: Without the annotation it compiled; that is what makes the typo dangerous.

prompt: `Item.copy()` returns `Item`. Which return type may `Book.copy()` declare?
hint: Every caller of the old signature must still get what it was promised.

choices.text: Only `Item`, exactly
choices.why: A subtype is allowed; `Book` used it.

choices.text: `Object`, since every class is one
choices.why: That widens the promise, and callers expecting an `Item` would break.

choices.text: `Item` or any subtype of it, such as `Book`
choices.why: Right: a covariant return narrows the type and keeps the promise.

choices.text: Any type, as long as the method is annotated
choices.why: `@Override` checks the rules; it does not relax them.

prompt: `Quiet` overrode the public `describe()` as `protected` and was refused. Why does Java forbid narrowing access?
hint: Think of code holding an `Item`.

choices.text: Code holding an `Item` was promised it could call `describe()`
choices.why: Right: a `Quiet` behind an `Item` variable would break that promise.

choices.text: Because `protected` methods cannot be overridden
choices.why: They can; the rule is about which direction access may move.

choices.text: Because a subclass must use the same access words as its parent
choices.why: Wider access is allowed; only narrower is refused.

prompt: Which of these would the compiler refuse in a subclass of `Item`? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table in section 03.

choices.text: `@Override public String descibe()`
choices.why: Yes: the annotation finds that it overrides nothing.

choices.text: `@Override public Book copy()`
choices.why: No: a covariant return is allowed.

choices.text: `@Override protected String describe()`
choices.why: Yes: weaker access than `public`.

choices.text: `@Override public Object copy()`
choices.why: Yes: `Object` is not `Item` nor a subtype of it.

choices.text: `public String describe(String prefix)` with no annotation
choices.why: No: that is a new overload, and legal.

prompt: `Book` declared `public boolean equals(Book other)`. What is that method, to the compiler?
hint: Compare its parameter with `Object`'s.

choices.text: An override of `Object.equals`
choices.why: An override needs the same parameter type, `Object`.

choices.text: An overload of `equals`
choices.why: Right: it sits beside the inherited `equals(Object)`, and `Book` ends up with two.

choices.text: A compile error, since `equals` may only take `Object`
choices.why: It compiled; that is why the mistake survives.

prompt: With `equals(Book)`, how many books did the `HashSet` hold after adding `a` and `b`, two books with the same ISBN?
hint: The second line of the first run.

prompt: Why did `HashSet` never call the `equals(Book)` Ana wrote?
hint: What type does `HashSet` know its elements as, when it is compiled?

choices.text: Because `HashSet` compares hash codes only, never `equals`
choices.why: It compares hash codes first and then calls `equals` on a match; both hash codes matched here.

choices.text: Its call was compiled as `equals(Object)`, which still meant `Object`'s identity check
choices.why: Right: overloads are chosen from declared types, and the set declares `Object`.

choices.text: Because `equals(Book)` is not public
choices.why: It was declared `public`.

choices.text: Because `a` and `b` have different titles
choices.why: Their titles were the same, and the rule compared ISBNs anyway.

prompt: What did `a.equals(asObject)` print with the first `Book`, where `asObject` is `b` held in an `Object` variable?
hint: The declared type of the argument chose the method.

choices.text: `a.equals(asObject): true`, since it is the same `b`
choices.why: Same object, different declared type, so a different method.

choices.text: `a.equals(asObject): false`
choices.why: Right: declared `Object`, so `equals(Object)`, so identity.

choices.text: A `ClassCastException`, since an `Object` is not a `Book`
choices.why: Nothing was cast; the inherited method accepted the `Object`.

prompt: Putting the annotation `@___` on `equals(Book)` turns the mistake into a compile error.
hint: It asks the compiler to confirm a method replaces one from a supertype.

prompt: The fixed `Book` overrides `equals(Object)` correctly but someone deletes its `hashCode`. Two books with the same ISBN go into a `HashSet`. What is the risk?
hint: Equal objects must have equal hash codes.

choices.text: The set looks for the second in the wrong place and keeps both
choices.why: Right: with identity hash codes the two land in different places and `equals` is never asked.

choices.text: None, since `equals` is now right
choices.why: `HashSet` only calls `equals` for elements whose hash codes lead to the same place.

choices.text: The program fails to compile without `hashCode`
choices.why: Every class inherits one from `Object`; the code compiles and misbehaves.

choices.text: `HashSet.add` throws because the hash codes differ
choices.why: Different hash codes are normal; the set simply files them apart.

prompt: Match each situation to what decides which method runs.
hint: Overloads are chosen by the compiler; overrides by the object.

pairs.right: The declared types of the arguments

right_distractors: The order the methods appear in the file

prompt: A `Member` class declares `public int compareTo(Member other)` but forgets `implements Comparable<Member>`. `members.sort(null)` throws a `ClassCastException`. What happened?
hint: A method with the right name is not a signed contract.

choices.text: `compareTo` was overloaded instead of overridden, as in the `equals` trap
choices.why: Close, but here there was nothing to override: `Member` signed no contract at all.

choices.text: `sort` casts each element to the interface, and that cast fails
choices.why: Right: the method exists, but only `implements` makes the class the type `sort` casts to.

choices.text: `compareTo` returned a negative number for equal members
choices.why: The cast failed before any comparison ran.

prompt: Which habit from this lesson would have caught both the `descibe` typo and the `equals(Book)` mistake?
hint: One annotation.

choices.text: Writing a unit test for every method
choices.why: Tests help, but the quick test of `a.equals(b)` passed.

choices.text: Avoiding overloads altogether
choices.why: Neither mistake was a deliberate overload.

choices.text: `@Override` on every method meant to replace one
choices.why: Right: in both cases the compiler would have said the method overrides nothing.
